34bce5a2-0de0-4988-af0d-0d33833565ee.recap: Kevin Coldiron interviews FT journalist Robin Wigglesworth about his new book on the history of bonds. Most of the conversation traces how bond market 'technology' built state power: Venice's 12th-century forced war loan (prestiti) became the first tradable bond and later consolidated into a single homogeneous issue (monte), Britain's consolidated annuities became arguably the first reserve asset because parliamentary checks on the crown made repayment credible, and the post-WWII Eurodollar glut (dollars pooling offshore, partly from Soviet-bloc banks) seeded the stateless Eurobond market that rebuilt London as a financial center. A long section covers Michael Milken, who read economist Braddock Hickman's finding that diversified low-rated bonds outperform after defaults, then built an original-issue junk bond market (rather than just trading fallen angels) at Drexel Burnham Lambert, birthing the modern leveraged finance and private credit industry -- though later vintages of junk defaulted more as quality diluted. Wigglesworth argues fixed-income ETFs have unexpectedly improved bond market liquidity rather than harming it, interacting with electronification and portfolio trading, and flags tokenization (already growing in repo) as an underappreciated coming shift. The interview closes on current events: Treasury Secretary Bessent's expanded liquidity buybacks, which Wigglesworth dismisses as largely symbolic ('peeing on a forest fire') relative to total issuance, but acknowledges are aimed at dampening volatility to protect hedge funds' heavily levered Treasury basis trade -- with the real fix being Fed chair Kevin Warsh signaling openness to rate hikes to rein in above-target inflation and rising term premium.
terms: Eurodollar -- offshore US dollar deposits/bonds held outside the US banking system
basis trade -- levered arbitrage going long Treasury cash bonds and short Treasury futures to capture the price difference
term premium -- extra yield investors demand for holding longer-dated bonds over expected short-rate path
fallen angel -- a bond originally issued investment-grade that is later downgraded to junk
